TEXT: European markets showed tentative signs of recovery after a rough few days, with modest gains in precious metals, tech stocks, and cryptocurrencies. Silver recovered 4% to $74.18 after falling 13% to near $64, while gold rose 2% to $4,882 from a low of $4,655. US equities and futures also showed early signs of recovery, with the S&P 500 futures up 0.5%. The US dollar remained steady, and WTI crude oil was flat at $63.16 amid ongoing US-Iran negotiations. Overall, the markets are experiencing volatility but are correcting.

Oil markets experienced initial gains following news of prolonged U.S.-Iran nuclear negotiations, with Brent and WTI Crude prices rising to $68 and $64 per barrel respectively. However, prices later declined as investors interpreted the talks as a preliminary step rather than a resolution. The talks, led by U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi, aim to establish a roadmap for further discussions, with Iran emphasizing good faith and firm stances on rights.
Oil prices are expected to see their first weekly decline in weeks, with Brent crude and WTI rising 1.1% to $68.28, as markets anticipate U.S.-Iran talks.

Russian crude discounts to China have reached record levels as sellers reduce prices to maintain demand amidst the risk of losing Indian buyers due to a US-India trade agreement. China’s independent refiners are absorbing displaced Russian barrels, benefiting from deeper discounts and higher margins. However, China's capacity to take additional Russian crude is limited, with state refiners still sidelined. The market now focuses on whether further discounting can sustain flows or if oversupply pressures will intensify.

European markets saw gold and silver decline amid a selloff in Asia, with silver dropping over 13%. The Bank of England maintained its interest rate at 3.75%, signaling a dovish stance. The USD/JPY pair approached the intervention level, while Bitcoin fell below the $70,000 mark. US January Challenger layoffs were announced, and Eurozone retail sales declined. Germany's industrial orders rose, and UK construction PMI showed improvement. Markets remained focused on precious metals, with WTI crude oil experiencing volatility.

Despite macroeconomic challenges, geopolitical shifts, and volatile oil prices affecting M&A activity in the oil & gas industry through 2025, dealmaking showed signs of recovery in the latter part of the year. As we move into 2026, there is hope that the green shoots of deal activity will continue to strengthen, although the outlook for M&A remains dependent on commodity prices. With oil prices currently below $70 per barrel, the appetite for selling assets or companies is likely to remain muted. However, the majority of exploration and production (E&P) companies and midstream players remain profitable, leading to opportunistic deals rather than distressed M&A.

Oil prices surged and then dropped sharply as reports of cancelled Iran-US talks caused market volatility. The initial jump reflected fears of renewed escalation, but prices quickly fell after Iran confirmed the talks were still set for Friday in Oman. Despite the confirmation, markets remained unstable due to unresolved differences over the agenda, with Iran focusing on nuclear issues and the US seeking broader discussions including missile and regional activities.

Software stocks faced a significant re-rating after fears of lost pricing power, with MU and AMD falling 9% and 16% respectively. Bitcoin hit a new low at $72,082, dragging down markets. Industrial and transport sectors showed strength amidst the downturn. The US dollar strengthened, while the yen struggled ahead of an election. A shadow fleet of tankers is covertly transporting sanctioned oil, bypassing international sanctions and contributing up to 7% of global crude flows. In 2025, these vessels moved an estimated 3.7 billion barrels, significantly impacting global energy markets and oil prices.

European markets saw a recovery with gold and silver prices rising, while the US dollar remained mixed. Markets also focused on the ECB's interest rate decisions, with the 2.2% inflation reading not indicating an imminent rate cut.

European energy giants like Shell and TotalEnergies face a challenging earnings season with shareholder returns at risk due to lower crude prices. Analysts predict the lowest fourth-quarter profits in nearly five years for these companies. Industry experts suggest that while dividends may remain unchanged, buybacks and capital programs could be reduced, potentially affecting low-carbon projects and exploration efforts. A private survey by the American Petroleum Institute (API) indicates a significant draw in headline crude oil inventories, contrasting with expectations of a slight increase. The API report, a preliminary indicator, is based on voluntary submissions and is released before the more comprehensive and authoritative data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA). The EIA's mandatory data collection provides a detailed snapshot of oil market conditions, including refinery inputs and outputs, and is considered the definitive reference for traders and analysts. Discrepancies between the API and EIA reports can cause short-term volatility in oil prices as markets reassess supply-demand balances.

The US House voted to end the government shutdown, while the Fed's Barkin and Miran provided mixed views on inflation and rate cuts. The US military shot down an Iranian drone near an aircraft carrier. Gold and silver saw significant gains, with gold reaching a $275 one-day nominal gain. Tech stocks and crypto experienced volatility, with Bitcoin recovering from a low. The Australian dollar continued its rise post-rate hike, while the yen saw no change. The S&P 500 fell by 0.8%, and the AUD/JPY pair showed strong performance.

Wall Street saw stocks fall as geopolitical tensions in the Middle East resurfaced, while gold surged more than 6% to $4,950 per ounce, marking its strongest session since November 2008. The rally in gold and silver came after two days of significant selling, driven by concerns over potential restrictive monetary policy following Kevin Warsh's appointment as the next Federal Reserve chair. Energy markets also reacted to renewed tensions, with crude oil rising 1.8% to $63 a barrel after U.S. officials reported shooting down an Iranian drone.

President Trump announced a U.S. trade deal with India, promising India will stop buying Russian oil, but data shows shadow fleet vessels continue unloading sanctioned Russian crude at Indian ports. Four tankers associated with Russia's shadow fleet were tracked unloading oil at various Indian refineries. Despite U.S. enforcement efforts, the global shadow fleet, estimated at 1,400 vessels, continues to navigate around sanctions, with some tankers completing deliveries to China and others facing seizures by European nations.

Oil markets are influenced by political uncertainty, with Trump's mixed messages on Iran and India's stance on Russian crude affecting prices. Despite 2026 being labeled the year of oversupply, January oil prices matched last year's levels, defying demand predictions. Trump's fluctuating comments on Iran have revived oil's geopolitical premium, leading to increased open interest in ICE Brent futures and bullish positioning by hedge funds. Equinor sold its Argentine shale business to Vista Energy, and Shell's Nigerian subsidiary plans to suspend production at the Bonga field.

January saw a broad rally across global assets, with equities, commodities, and precious metals performing well despite geopolitical risks. The S&P 500 briefly surpassed 7,000, and the MSCI EM index had its best monthly performance since November 2022. Gold and silver saw significant gains, with gold's best monthly performance since September 1999. Brent crude oil reached $70.69/bbl, its highest monthly jump in four years. India's suspension of Russian crude oil imports, following a deal with the U.S. to reduce tariffs in exchange for increased American oil purchases, threatens to disrupt global markets. Moody's warns of major disruptions, as India seeks alternatives due to U.S. sanctions on Russian companies. Indian refiners are increasing non-Russian oil imports, potentially reaching a record 5.2 million barrels per day, which could offset the decline in Russian crude imports.

India's potential suspension of Russian crude oil imports, following a trade deal with the U.S., could disrupt global markets, warns Moody's. The deal, announced by President Trump, includes reduced U.S. tariffs on Indian goods in exchange for India's commitment to stop buying Russian oil and increase American oil purchases. The agreement may also provide access to Venezuelan and possibly Iranian crude, as India seeks alternatives to Russian oil, which has been its largest supplier for four years.

Sarah Ferguson's crude remark about her daughter, Princess Eugenie, in a 2010 email surfaced in newly released Jeffrey Epstein documents. Ferguson, who divorced Prince Andrew in 1996, had previously reached out to Epstein in 2011 after denouncing their friendship. The Department of Justice released over 3 million Epstein records, including personal emails, revealing Ferguson's comment about Eugenie returning from a 'shagging weekend.' President Donald Trump announced a reduction of tariffs on Indian goods to 18% after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi agreed to cease purchasing Russian oil. This decision follows months of Trump urging India to reduce its reliance on Russian crude amid global efforts to isolate Moscow for its invasion of Ukraine. The tariff cut is part of a broader trade agreement, with India also agreeing to reduce import taxes on U.S. goods to zero and purchase $500 billion worth of American products. The move aims to support the war effort in Ukraine and strengthen U.S.-India relations, which have been strained by trade disputes and Russia's actions in Ukraine.

Crude oil prices dropped by 5% to $61.98, and gold declined by 0.9% to $4,704.70. European markets also saw gains, with the STOXX 600 rising 1% and Spain's IBEX 35 Index up by 1.2%.

The Trump administration is reportedly engaging in back-channel talks through Turkey and Qatar, with the White House open to negotiations and Tehran showing interest in nuclear talks. The longer-term odds of a strike by June 30 are at 54%, with traders noting Iran's greater complexity as a target compared to Venezuela.

Global stock futures decline amid a selloff in metals and Bitcoin, with S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures down 0.4% and 0.8% respectively. European stocks rebound slightly, while Asian markets retreat due to risk-off sentiment. Gold, silver, and oil prices fall, with Bitcoin hitting a 10-month low. The decision involves eight member countries and comes despite a recent rise in oil prices, which have since dropped following President Trump's comments on Iran's willingness to negotiate. Analysts are questioning the oversupply narrative, noting that the timespreads suggest a smaller surplus than expected.

Oil prices dropped by more than 5% amid signs of easing tensions between the US and Iran, with President Trump suggesting serious talks are underway. The Brent Crude benchmark fell to $65 per barrel, down from a five-month high of $70, while the US benchmark, WTI Crude, was at $61.92. The decline followed President Trump's comments that Iran is 'seriously' negotiating with the US, potentially leading to an acceptable deal, and his refusal to confirm a military strike despite sending a large naval force to the Persian Gulf.

President Donald Trump announced that China could strike a deal with the U.S. to purchase Venezuelan oil, while also suggesting India is already making such a deal. This follows Trump's 25% tariff on Venezuelan oil imports, which led India to stop buying from Venezuela. Venezuelan crude is important for China's asphalt production, and the U.S. is looking to redirect these imports away from Iran.

The U.S. and Taiwan have signed a trade deal lowering tariffs on Taiwanese exports to 15% and opening Taiwan's market to U.S. goods. The agreement includes a $84 billion purchase commitment from Taiwan for U.S. goods from 2025 to 2029, covering items like liquefied natural gas, crude oil, aircraft, and power equipment. Taiwan will eliminate or reduce 99% of tariff barriers on U.S. goods and provide preferential market access for U.S. industrial and agricultural exports. The deal also includes commitments from Taiwanese tech and chip firms to invest $250 billion in U.S. production capacity.

Crude oil and gasoline prices fell sharply on Thursday, with March WTI crude oil down -1.79% and March RBOB gasoline down -3.18%. The decline was driven by a risk-off sentiment in asset markets, long liquidation in energy futures, and mounting crude supplies in floating storage. The International Energy Agency (IEA) has revised its oil demand growth forecast for 2026, predicting an increase of 850,000 barrels per day, down from the previous estimate of 930,000 bpd. The growth is expected to be driven by developing economies, with China leading the additional demand. Petrochemical feedstock products are projected to account for more than half of the year's gains, a shift from the previous year's dominance by transport fuels. The IEA's forecast is lower than OPEC's estimate of 1.4 million bpd growth and anticipates a surplus in the oil market in 2026, with supply rising by 2.4 million bpd. The IEA also noted that global oil supply was significantly impacted by severe winter weather in January but expects a rebound in the coming months.

U.S. refiners Marathon Petroleum, Valero Energy Corp., and Phillips 66 reported earnings that exceeded expectations, benefiting from a glut of cheap crude oil. The surplus in global fuel markets, with demand outpacing new refining capacity, allows refiners to purchase cheaper feedstock and sell finished fuels at higher prices. Phillips 66 CEO Mark Lashier expressed optimism for the industry's future, contrasting the current bullish outlook with the uncertainty faced in early 2025. Refining margins for these companies increased by about $5 a barrel in 2025 compared to the previous year, with strong fuel demand forecasted to continue driving profits.

Argus, a global energy and commodity price reporting agency, has launched the first assessed prices for Venezuelan crude following the reopening of the country's oil market and the lifting of western sanctions. The new assessments cover the price of Venezuelan crude at the US Gulf coast, where much of the oil will be delivered. The three crudes assessed—Merey, Hamaca, and Boscan—are based on cargoes delivered by Aframax tankers to refineries and terminals in that region. Venezuelan crude exports had fallen to 700,000 b/d due to sanctions but are expected to rise to as much as 1mn b/d by the end of this year. Argus' assessments are crucial for settling a large and complex web of physical and derivative contracts in the US Gulf coast crude market.

Argus, a global energy and commodity price reporting agency, has released the first assessed prices for Venezuelan crude since the lifting of western sanctions and reopening of the country's oil market to US buyers. The assessments cover three Venezuelan crudes—Merey, Hamaca, and Boscan—delivered by Aframax tankers to the US Gulf coast. Venezuelan crude exports, which had dwindled to 700,000 barrels per day (b/d) due to sanctions, are expected to rise to 1 million b/d by year-end. China was the largest consumer of Venezuelan oil last year, but with sanctions lifted, more crude is likely to enter the US Gulf coast market, competing with Canadian heavy grades.

Hedge funds have increased bullish bets on crude oil, with net-long Brent crude positions rising by over 31,000 contracts to nearly 278,000 lots, the highest in about ten months. This shift, driven by geopolitical tensions surrounding Iran, marks a return to supply-focused trading after a period of defensive stances. Data from the Commodity Futures Trading Commission indicates that money managers also raised net-long positions in WTI crude to a six-month high. The move suggests traders are prioritizing geopolitical risk premiums over inventory trends or near-term demand signals, with the strongest increase seen in Brent contracts.

Goldman Sachs predicts Brent crude oil could fall to $40 per barrel by late 2026 due to Iran sanctions, OPEC+ production increases, and trade-war-driven recession risks. The base case forecasts Brent averaging $63 in 2025 and $58 in 2026, while the worst-case scenario envisions a significant economic downturn and collapse in OPEC+ discipline, reminiscent of the 2020 pandemic-era crash. The reimposition of US sanctions on Iranian oil exports adds complexity to the market, potentially reducing Iran's oil revenue and impacting global supply.
